name: MoE Run Anyway Edge Hardware Quickstart
scope: Feasibility guidance for edge and local hardware targets.
Small-model routing is the near-term path: route among small dense models, small MoEs, and smoke models at the harness layer before attempting true expert paging.
Hardware tiers are compatibility and planning tiers, not guaranteed support statements.
Phone emulators are API, UI, client, and packaging smoke targets; they do not replace real mobile GPU, NPU, memory, battery, or thermal testing.
safety_contract: Planner does not launch model servers.
Planner does not send prompt traffic.

near_term: Route by task family, prompt family, latency budget, memory budget, and hardware tier.
Treat small dense models as routable experts or subagents at the harness layer.
Record router decisions, selected model class, artifact labels, fallback use, timing, and runtime evidence separately.
Do not claim semantic expert routing unless trace artifacts expose router outputs, expert ids, and layer/window metadata.
later: Connect harness-level routing to true MoE expert paging only after a runtime actuator proves expert inventory, residency observation, residency control, fallback, cleanup, and artifact export.
Use Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Mixtral, or larger MoE targets only where memory and runtime evidence make them plausible.

runtime_families.notes: Useful for CPU, Apple Silicon, CUDA/ROCm, Jetson builds, and Android experiments when a compatible binary exists. Stock endpoint telemetry is runtime evidence, not semantic expert routing.
Useful for passive sidecar and baseline readiness when a user-managed local endpoint already exists.
Practical local dense-model route target where installed by the user; MoE internals are generally not exposed.
Useful for server-class GPU baselines and some OpenAI-compatible flows; semantic expert ids require explicit runtime support.
Preferred semantic trace path when a model remains hookable and local dependencies already exist.
Candidate mobile and edge runtime family; treat as a compatibility target until artifact support is proven.
Candidate mobile and edge runtime family for small dense models; not an expert-paging actuator by itself.
Candidate Apple Silicon family for unified-memory dense or smaller MoE experiments.
Candidate NVIDIA edge family when the target device has compatible JetPack, CUDA, and memory headroom.
Client and smoke-test target only; not a substitute for real Android GPU/NPU or thermal testing.

model_classes.routing_role: Exercise harness shape, artifact labels, fallback paths, and client compatibility.

model_classes.display_name: Small dense models as routable experts/subagents
model_classes.routing_role: Near-term practical path: choose a small model by task family, latency budget, and device budget.
Single-model baseline or one of several route targets on stronger local devices.

model_classes.display_name: Small MoE or MoE-shaped smoke models
model_classes.routing_role: Validate semantic trace shape when hooks expose router outputs.
Large sparse target for high-memory local tests only after baseline readiness and memory headroom are proven.
MoE-class target for stronger GPUs or high-memory CPU/Apple Silicon hosts when runtime support is available.
Higher-memory MoE baseline target; stock endpoints still do not prove semantic expert routing.

hardware_tiers.minimum_memory: 32GB system RAM for small dense smoke tests; 64GB+ for larger quantized dense or MoE feasibility checks.
hardware_tiers.comfortable_memory: 96GB to 128GB+ system RAM when testing Mixtral-class or DeepSeek-V2-Lite-class quantized targets slowly.
storage_notes: Keep at least 2x the largest model file size free for downloads performed outside this repo, conversions, and run artifacts.
Use SSD storage for large GGUF or checkpoint files; HDD-backed paging can dominate timings.
context_kv_cache_notes: Long context can exceed model-weight memory through KV cache growth.
Reduce context, batch, parallel slots, and prompt count before interpreting failures as model incompatibility.
risk_notes: CPU-only runs can be valid compatibility baselines while still being too slow for product use.
Operating-system swap may make a run appear feasible while hiding unusable latency.
hardware_tiers.recommended_first_test: Run baseline readiness planning, then a tiny/smoke route with short context and explicit artifact labels.

hardware_tiers.minimum_memory: 8GB VRAM plus 16GB to 32GB system RAM for small dense quantized targets.
hardware_tiers.comfortable_memory: Small dense 0.5B-7B quantized route targets; leave headroom for KV cache and display memory.
storage_notes: Reserve SSD space for multiple small candidate models if comparing routed experts.
Avoid assuming a model fits because the weight file is below 8GB.
context_kv_cache_notes: KV cache, graph buffers, batch size, and concurrent slots can push an apparently fitting model over the edge.
Start with short context and one slot.
risk_notes: This tier is better for routing among small dense experts than for large MoE paging.
Partial CPU offload may work but can change latency enough to affect routing decisions.
hardware_tiers.recommended_first_test: Compare two or three small dense models as harness-level experts with the same prompt family and short context.

hardware_tiers.minimum_memory: 12GB VRAM plus 32GB system RAM for small and medium dense quantized tests.
hardware_tiers.comfortable_memory: 7B-14B dense quantized targets or several small dense route targets, depending on context length.
storage_notes: Plan storage for model variants at different quantization levels.
Keep baseline artifacts separate by model, quantization, context, and runtime.
context_kv_cache_notes: Context length remains a first-class memory budget item.
Router comparisons should pin context and batch settings before comparing latency.
risk_notes: Some sparse models may load only with aggressive quantization or CPU spill.
Do not infer semantic expert selection from timing differences.
hardware_tiers.recommended_first_test: Run a small-model routing matrix by prompt family, latency budget, and artifact label; defer larger MoE tests until readiness artifacts are stable.

hardware_tiers.minimum_memory: 16GB VRAM plus 32GB to 64GB system RAM for medium dense targets and limited sparse smoke tests.
hardware_tiers.comfortable_memory: Several small dense experts or one larger quantized dense target with moderate context.
storage_notes: Store one baseline bundle per candidate route target.
Track quantization, GPU layers, context, and offload settings in labels.
context_kv_cache_notes: Long context and parallel slots can be the limiting factor even when weights fit.
Use small context for first-pass routing evidence.
risk_notes: DeepSeek-V2-Lite-class targets are feasibility candidates, not default assumptions.
Runtime support and quantization quality matter as much as nominal VRAM.
hardware_tiers.recommended_first_test: Capture runtime baseline readiness, then test small dense expert routing before trying a sparse target.

hardware_tiers.minimum_memory: 24GB VRAM plus 64GB system RAM for larger dense quantized and selected sparse feasibility tests.
hardware_tiers.comfortable_memory: 14B dense, multiple small dense route targets, and some Qwen3-30B-A3B or DeepSeek-V2-Lite quantized experiments.
storage_notes: Expect tens of GB per larger sparse or dense model variant.
Keep failed-load manifests; memory failures are useful compatibility evidence.
context_kv_cache_notes: KV cache can decide whether Qwen3-30B-A3B-class tests fit.
Run short-context smoke tests before increasing context.
risk_notes: Mixtral-class feasibility depends on quantization, offload split, runtime, and context.
Large sparse tests still need trace evidence before any semantic expert-routing claim.
hardware_tiers.recommended_first_test: Run a routed small-dense baseline first, then a short-context sparse smoke load with artifact labels that separate runtime and semantic evidence.

hardware_tiers.minimum_memory: 48GB VRAM plus 128GB system RAM for comfortable larger sparse-model feasibility work.
hardware_tiers.comfortable_memory: 48GB to 80GB+ VRAM for Mixtral-class, DeepSeek-V2-Lite-class, Qwen3-30B-A3B-class, and richer route comparisons.
storage_notes: Plan hundreds of GB if retaining multiple checkpoints, quantizations, traces, and baseline bundles.
Separate model cache storage from artifact output storage where possible.
context_kv_cache_notes: High VRAM does not remove the need to label context, batch, parallel slots, and KV-cache policy.
Long-context comparisons should be a separate test axis from model routing.
risk_notes: Server-class memory makes larger baselines plausible but does not prove actuator control.
Hookable runtimes are still required for semantic traces unless the serving runtime exposes router outputs.
hardware_tiers.recommended_first_test: Capture baseline readiness and run a small routed suite, then compare one larger sparse target with explicit trace-evidence labels.

hardware_tiers.minimum_memory: 16GB unified memory for small dense smoke tests; 32GB+ for more useful local routing; 64GB+ for larger sparse feasibility.
hardware_tiers.comfortable_memory: 32GB to 128GB unified memory, depending on model size, context, and runtime.
storage_notes: Model files and converted artifacts can consume large local SSD space quickly.
Record runtime family because llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML paths expose different evidence.
context_kv_cache_notes: Unified memory avoids a hard VRAM boundary but not total memory pressure.
Thermal throttling can affect latency budgets during repeated routing tests.
risk_notes: Unified memory capacity is shared with the OS and applications.
Larger MoE tests are feasibility targets and may require aggressive quantization.
hardware_tiers.recommended_first_test: Use small dense route targets first, then test larger sparse candidates only with short context and clear memory labels.

hardware_tiers.minimum_memory: 8GB unified/device memory for tiny smoke models; 16GB+ for small dense routing; 32GB+ for more useful edge experiments.
hardware_tiers.comfortable_memory: Orin-class 32GB to 64GB devices for sustained small dense routing and selected optimized sparse feasibility checks.
storage_notes: Use fast local storage where available; removable media can distort timings.
Retain build/runtime metadata such as JetPack, CUDA, TensorRT, and architecture.
context_kv_cache_notes: Edge memory is shared across runtime, OS, display, and other services.
Sustained thermal and power modes matter for repeatability.
risk_notes: Build compatibility can dominate model compatibility.
Thermal throttling makes emulator or desktop results poor predictors.
hardware_tiers.recommended_first_test: Run an edge smoke route with tiny or small dense models, recording power mode, context, runtime, and artifact labels.

hardware_tiers.minimum_memory: Emulator: enough host RAM for client smoke tests. Real phone: device-specific memory and accelerator limits, usually tiny or small dense only.
hardware_tiers.comfortable_memory: Real high-end devices with enough RAM and supported runtime for small dense local inference; emulator for API/UI/client compatibility only.
storage_notes: Emulator storage checks are packaging and file-access checks, not proof of phone storage performance.
Real devices need available app storage and model placement planned explicitly.
context_kv_cache_notes: Mobile KV cache, thermal limits, and battery constraints can dominate feasibility.
Use tiny context for first tests and increase only after real-device evidence.
risk_notes: Emulator smoke tests do not validate real mobile GPU, NPU, memory bandwidth, battery, or thermal behavior.
A passing emulator test is only compatibility evidence unless repeated on real hardware.
hardware_tiers.recommended_first_test: Use the emulator for client/API smoke, then repeat a tiny real-device route before claiming mobile feasibility.

recommended_test_path.description: Capture or plan baseline readiness from local manifests without endpoint checks or prompt traffic.
Run a tiny or small dense route only after explicit runtime approval; keep prompt family, context, and route labels fixed.
Compare selected model class, router decision, fallback use, runtime family, timing, and artifact labels.
Do not claim semantic expert routing unless trace evidence includes router outputs, expert ids, and layer/window metadata.
